Line of effort

Using AI to test many approaches, fast

In shortAI can search thousands of combinations of approaches, play subject and clinician in simulation, and run around the clock. Only people approve what gets tested on people.

This program has more promising ideas than ordinary studies can test. Catalysts, workflows, memory aids, and emotion skills combine into thousands of possible packages, and the best one likely differs from person to person. This line of effort uses AI, including agentic AI (systems that plan and carry out multi-step work under human supervision), to search those combinations quickly and safely. AI can also stand in as both subject and clinician in simulated studies, run continuously, and hand its most promising ideas, including medicine-related ones, to people to test.

What AI can do

Keep the evidence review continuously up to date, design efficient experiments, decide in real time which approach each participant tries next (using rules fixed in advance), and spot patterns in who benefits. This can shrink years of one-at-a-time trials into months.

What AI cannot do

Prove that something works without real people testing it. Testing many combinations also raises the chance of lucky false positives, so every AI-selected winner must repeat in a fresh group of people before it counts. AI does not diagnose, change medication, or replace clinicians.

The clinical assessment plan: five problems to target first

Each problem gets its own measures and its own set of approaches to combine. Everyone also completes regular mood and safety check-ins.

ProblemHow it is assessedApproaches to combineWhat counts as better
Starting tasksTask initiationStarting delay from app logs and phone check-ins; procrastination questionnairesCatalysts, zero-friction staging, writing the next action, ignition starters, outside deadlinesFewer minutes between planning to start and actually starting
Remembering to do thingsWorking and prospective memoryMemory-span tasks; tasks that test remembering to act later; a memory-slips questionnaire; real reminders sent by phone"When X, I do Y" plans, reminder timing and type, offloading to lists, spaced repetitionMore intended actions done on time
Pain from rejectionRejection sensitivityA rejection-sensitivity questionnaire; an emotion-regulation questionnaire; mood ratings after real social setbacksReframing prompts, self-compassion exercises, naming the emotion, a pause-before-replying rule, brief educationFaster mood recovery and less intense distress after a setback
Staying with itSustained attention and timeReaction-time consistency; mind-wandering checks; time-estimation tasksMicro-sprints, visible timers, white or pink noise, movement breaksLonger time on task; less mind-wandering
Sleep and body clockArousal and rhythmWearable sleep tracking; a body-clock questionnaireMorning light, wind-down routines, regular sleep timesMore regular sleep and easier starts the next day

"Rejection sensitive dysphoria" is a widely used clinical term, popularized by William Dodson, but it is not a formal diagnosis and has no validated test. The program measures rejection sensitivity and emotional reactivity, which research shows are higher on average in ADHD.

How the search works

Eight approaches, each on or off, make 256 combinations. A well-designed screening experiment can estimate the effect of each approach, and the main ways they combine, from just 32 of them.

  1. Months 0–3

    Evidence engine

    AI agents keep a living map of the research on every candidate approach for each problem. People check every decision, because AI screening is fast but misses studies.

  2. Months 2–4

    Shortlist

    Rank combinations using prior evidence and simple models. Drop ones that are redundant, burdensome, or risky.

  3. Months 4–9

    Screening experiments

    Online studies test many approaches at once using efficient factorial designs. Low-risk approaches only, adults only, with ethics review.

  4. Months 9–18

    Personalize

    Phone-based studies in which a pre-set learning algorithm finds which approach helps which person in which situation. Each participant gets a personal report.

  5. Academic phase

    Sequence and confirm

    Test what to do next when something doesn't work, then test the best personalized package against usual care in a randomized trial across diagnoses.

AI agents and the people who oversee them

Show the six AI roles

Evidence agent

Searches, screens, and summarizes studies. People verify every inclusion and every number.

Design agent

Drafts experiments and simulates how many participants are needed. A statistician signs off.

Allocation engine

Decides who tries what next, using only rules registered in advance. It cannot rewrite its own rules.

Analysis agent

Runs the planned analyses and flags anything unusual. Unplanned findings are labeled as exploratory.

Participant assistant

Sends prompts and scripted, low-risk coaching. It is not a therapist. Any sign of crisis goes straight to a person, with crisis contacts shown.

Safety monitor

Watches mood scores and side effects and can pause a study arm. People decide what happens next.

AI as subject and as clinician

Before a real person tries anything, the program can run its studies in simulation, with AI playing both roles. Simulation can only suggest what to test with people. It is never evidence that something works.

AI as the subject

Simulated participants take part in virtual versions of each study. Some are computational models of motivation and attention, like a full version of the model above. Others are AI agents given realistic profiles. They can try thousands of catalyst sequences overnight. But AI "participants" that reproduce some classic findings also flatten and misrepresent real groups of people. So each simulated subject must first reproduce published results it has not seen, and is used only to decide what to test next.

AI as the clinician

An AI clinician agent runs the assessment plan on simulated subjects: it asks the questions, scores the measures, and chooses the next step. This stress-tests the protocol before any real person sees it, catching unclear questions, missed risk signs, and poor sequences. Conversational AI has matched doctors in some simulated diagnostic consultations, but with real participants, clinical decisions stay with human clinicians.

Sequencing catalysts, medicines, and supplements

Daily life mixes things together: a catalyst on a morning when medication is working, or after a bad night's sleep. The simulation layer explores order and timing: which catalyst to try first, what to switch to when it fades, and how catalysts might combine with prescribed medication or supplements. The most promising sequences become designs for real sequencing trials.

The program never tells anyone to start, stop, or re-time a medicine or supplement. Those decisions belong with the person's prescriber. Information about medication comes only from consenting participants' own reports and from published registry studies.

Looking for new medicines

Fastest route

Repurpose existing drugs

AI models that link conditions, genes, and approved drugs can rank existing medicines for new uses. Large registry studies, like the Swedish analyses of ADHD medication, can then check for real-world signals before any trial is considered.

Hypothesis stage

Learn from what already works

Current ADHD medicines act mainly on dopamine and noradrenaline. AI can help map why they help some people and not others, and which brain targets the engagement research points to remain untried.

Long road

Design new compounds

Generative chemistry and protein-structure prediction can propose and screen candidate molecules on a computer. AI-discovered drugs have done well in early safety trials, but succeed in effectiveness trials at about the usual rate. One has reached a successful mid-stage trial, in lung disease.

The program does no chemistry or drug testing itself. Promising candidates go to licensed academic and industry partners for laboratory work and regulated trials, which take years. AI drug design can also be misused to propose harmful molecules, so the search excludes look-alikes of controlled substances, screens for abuse potential and toxicity, and goes through biosafety review.

An engine that never stops, with people at the gates

The AI side can run around the clock, surfacing only the ideas most likely to pay off. People decide what happens to them.

Human gates

A scientific review board meets weekly. Approved ideas then pass ethics review, a small human pilot, and, for anything clinical or pharmaceutical, licensed partners and regulators. AI can propose and rank. Only people can approve a study, contact a participant, or move a compound forward.

Keeping the engine honest

The engine is graded on whether its "high probability" picks actually succeed with real people. If its forecasts turn out overconfident, its bar for surfacing ideas rises automatically, and every result, good or bad, feeds back into the next cycle.

Safeguards

Fast, but not careless

  • Ethics review and public preregistration before any study starts.
  • Every winning approach must repeat in a new group of people before it is recommended.
  • Collect only the data needed, process on the phone where possible, and never use participant data to train outside AI models.
  • Check results for bias across age, gender, ethnicity, and diagnosis.
  • Any tool that claims to diagnose or treat is reviewed against medical-device rules before release.
  • Simulated subjects and AI clinicians are used only to choose what to test, never as evidence.
  • Drug-discovery work excludes controlled-substance look-alikes and goes through biosafety review.

One randomized trial found that a carefully built AI therapy chatbot reduced depression and anxiety symptoms, but evidence on the safety of AI in mental health is still early. That is why AI here stays limited to low-risk support under human oversight.
